summary: Outlines architectural guidelines for developing Multipath TCP, which uses multiple paths at once for efficiency, resilience and throughput. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Rules of thumb for building TCP that sends one conversation along several roads at once.

questions: how big should the mptcp receive buffer be
subtitle: The goals and key design choices behind Multipath TCP, which spreads one connection over several paths.

tldr.problem: Hosts often have several network paths but a TCP connection uses only one. Using them together would add resilience and capacity, but the result must still look like TCP to applications and to middleboxes.
tldr.mechanism: Multipath TCP runs ordinary TCP subflows, one per path, under an MPTCP layer that keeps a connection-level sequence space, connection-level acknowledgements, TCP-option signaling and coupled congestion control.
tldr.outcome: The RFC sets goals and records the high-level design decisions behind MPTCP so it can be deployed through today's middleboxes. It is Informational.

facts.label: Buffer example
facts.value: 12.5 MB for 100 Mb/s, 10 ms plus 1 Mb/s, 1000 ms

today: RFC 6182 is Informational and, per the metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes the architecture, with the threat analysis in RFC 6181.

sections.title: Why Multipath Transport
sections.content:
Internet resources, especially bandwidth, often go unused because of protocol limits. Multipath transport uses several disjoint or partly disjoint paths at once, following the idea of resource pooling. The two key benefits are resilience, because one path can fail, and efficiency, because more network capacity is available to the end hosts.

Multipath TCP does this inside one transport connection, transparently to the application, mainly where one or both hosts are multihomed. The RFC has three purposes: to describe goals for a multipath transport, to lay out an architectural basis, and to document the high-level design decisions made for MPTCP. Companion documents cover the protocol extensions, congestion control and application issues.
sections.plainLanguage: If one road is crowded or closed, use another. Together, the roads carry more cars and stay open when one breaks.

sections.title: Goals
sections.content:
The functional goals are to improve throughput and resilience. A multipath connection SHOULD do no worse than a single TCP connection over the best path, and MUST be no less resilient than regular TCP. Use should be negotiated automatically with fall back to single-path TCP.

Compatibility goals matter as much:

  • Application: the same TCP service model (in-order, reliable, byte-oriented) and a backward compatible API.
  • Network: it must look like TCP on the wire, preserve fate-sharing, and traverse firewalls, NATs and performance-enhancing proxies. It MUST fall back to regular TCP when a path is insurmountably incompatible, and SHOULD work over IPv4 and IPv6 interchangeably.
  • Other users: it MUST NOT unduly harm single-path TCP users at shared bottlenecks.

The security goal is a service no less secure than regular TCP. The RFC contrasts this with SCTP, which supports multiple addresses but is blocked by middleboxes and rarely chosen by applications.
sections.plainLanguage: The new way must be at least as fast and as safe as the old way, work with all the existing roads and toll booths, and not push other drivers off the road.

sections.title: Architecture and Functional Decomposition
sections.content:
The architecture borrows from Tng, which splits the transport layer into an application-oriented Semantic layer and a network-oriented Flow+Endpoint layer. MPTCP is the Semantic layer, keeping TCP-like global ordering and reliability end to end. Each subflow is an ordinary TCP flow, the Flow+Endpoint layer, which middleboxes can handle segment by segment.

MPTCP needs four functions:

  • Path management: detect and use multiple paths, using multiple IP addresses as the clue, and set up subflows.
  • Packet scheduling: split the byte stream into segments for subflows, using a data sequence mapping, and reorder at the receiver.
  • Subflow interface: each subflow is TCP with its own sequence numbers.
  • Congestion control: coordinate subflows so an MPTCP connection does not take more than a single-path TCP flow would at a shared bottleneck.
sections.plainLanguage: One manager hands out the packages to several delivery drivers, each of whom follows normal road rules. At the end, the manager puts the packages back in order.

sections.title: Sequence Numbers, Acknowledgements and Buffers
sections.content:
MPTCP uses two sequence spaces: a connection-level number and one per subflow. A single shared number would leave gaps that upset middleboxes such as intrusion detection systems and would stop the sender attributing losses to the right path. The data sequence mapping is the tuple (data sequence number, subflow sequence number, length), and all three must be sent whenever a mapping is conveyed.

MPTCP for the public Internet MUST have explicit connection-level acknowledgements as well as subflow ones. One reason is a transparent proxy that ACKs a segment and then crashes, which would otherwise stall a connection that has other working subflows. A segment MUST be retransmittable on a different subflow, while the lost segment SHOULD still be sent on the path that lost it.

For buffers, the RECOMMENDED receive buffer is 2*sum(BW_i)*RTT_max, where RTT_max is the largest RTT across subflows. The send buffer is the same size. With a 100 Mb/s, 10 ms path and a 1 Mb/s, 1000 ms path, that is 12.5 MB, so it may be better to use slow paths for backup only.
sections.plainLanguage: Each driver numbers their own trips, and the manager also keeps one master list so a lost package can be re-sent by a different driver.

sections.title: Signaling, Paths and Identification
sections.content:
MPTCP signals with TCP options, starting with an option on the SYN. Options are the traditional TCP mechanism, are easy for NAT helpers to parse and avoid head-of-line blocking and congestion control of ACKs sent in the payload. The drawbacks are limited space, possible dropping by middleboxes and no guarantee of reliability, so the design falls back to regular TCP if control data is lost.

Paths are inferred from (source, destination) address pairs, and each is identified by a five-tuple, which could later allow port-based balancing such as with ECMP. Either host SHOULD be able to add subflows, and MPTCP MUST cope with paths appearing and disappearing. Each connection also needs a locally unique connection identifier, like an ephemeral port number. MPTCP MUST NOT be used for applications that bind to a specific address or interface.

Congestion control must couple the subflows to meet three goals: improve throughput, do no harm to others, and move traffic off the most congested paths.
sections.plainLanguage: A small flag on the first message says "I can use many roads." If a toll booth strips the flag, everyone just uses one road like before.

sections.title: Middleboxes and Security
sections.content:
Section 7 lists middlebox behavior that could hurt MPTCP: NATs that rewrite addresses, performance-enhancing proxies that split connections and may ACK early, traffic normalizers that dislike holes in sequence space, firewalls that randomize sequence numbers, intrusion detection systems that may drop MPTCP connections, and content-aware firewalls that rewrite data. Any of them may drop or strip unknown TCP options, or split and coalesce segments.

The security discussion builds on RFC 6181. A multi-addressed MPTCP SHOULD confirm that the parties in a subflow handshake match the original connection, verify that the peer can receive traffic at a new address, and provide replay protection. It should keep the DoS protections of standard TCP, and avoid heavy computation before reaching ESTABLISHED.
sections.plainLanguage: Many helpers sit on the roads and sometimes change or throw away unusual labels, so the design has to be careful and able to fall back.

items.title: Throughput
items.text: No worse than one TCP connection over the best path.

items.title: Resilience
items.text: Segments can be sent and re-sent on any available path.

items.title: Application compatibility
items.text: Same in-order, reliable, byte-oriented service as TCP.

items.title: Network compatibility
items.text: Looks like TCP on the wire and falls back when needed.

items.title: Fairness
items.text: Must not unduly harm single-path TCP users.

items.title: Security
items.text: No less secure than regular TCP.
